demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
He is a 55-year-old African man who has spent most of his adult life painting other people's homes, schools, and storefronts. He likes work that leaves a visible result behind him. He says there is comfort in starting with stained, cracked walls and ending with a clean surface, something orderly and finished. Before his loss, he is known as steady and patient, the kind of man who wakes early, drinks tea with his wife, and leaves for work with his brushes wrapped carefully in old cloths. He and his younger brother speak nearly every day. Their lives are closely linked, not dramatic, just familiar: calls about money, family news, who is ill, who is getting married, what repairs need doing.

The death comes suddenly. His brother is killed in a road traffic accident on an ordinary afternoon. There is no warning, no chance to say goodbye, only a phone call that at first makes no sense to him. He remembers the voice on the other end sounding strangely calm, as if speaking through water. For several seconds he thinks there must be some mistake. Even after he reaches the hospital and sees his brother's body, his mind keeps resisting what is in front of him. He notices absurd details-the pattern on a blanket, the harsh shine of the floor, a nurse adjusting paperwork-and later these details return to him more vividly than anything anyone says.

In the first weeks after the burial, he moves as if under instruction. He helps receive visitors, greets relatives, sits through prayers, and accepts condolences with a face that feels borrowed. At night, when the house finally becomes quiet, the reality of the loss arrives with force. He lies awake hearing the telephone call again. Sometimes he sees his brother as he imagines him in the last moments of the accident, though he was not there. His mind fills in what he does not know. He feels ashamed that these images come so easily and more ashamed that he cannot stop them.

Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. He wakes sweating, heart pounding, already tense before he understands where he is. In the morning he is irritable and exhausted. Small noises startle him: a car braking outside, metal clattering from a worksite, his wife setting down a pot too hard. He begins avoiding the road where the accident happened, then avoiding busy roads altogether. If a job requires travel across town, he finds excuses to send someone else or turns it down. He tells himself he is just tired, but he knows his world is shrinking.

Painting, once the place where he could settle himself, becomes difficult. He climbs a ladder and suddenly feels exposed, unsteady, distracted by thoughts that arrive out of nowhere. The smell of turpentine reminds him of the hospital disinfectant, and for a moment he is back there again, staring at a floor that shines too brightly. He loses track of measurements. He has to repaint sections because his hand is less careful now. Customers notice he is quieter. If someone mentions an accident in conversation, he feels his chest tighten and his jaw lock. He nods and leaves the room if he can.

At home, his wife experiences him as present in body but far away in spirit. He sits for long periods without speaking, television on but unwatched. She asks what he is thinking, and he says, "Nothing," because the truth feels impossible to explain. He is thinking of the last missed call from his brother that morning. He is thinking he should have called back sooner. He is thinking that a younger brother should not die first. He is thinking that if life can split open in one afternoon, then no ordinary day can be trusted. Their children tell him he seems harder now. He hears this and feels both defensive and defeated.

He no longer attends weddings and community gatherings the way he used to. Crowds drain him. Laughter can sound almost offensive, as if other people have forgotten some essential truth about how fragile life is. At the same time, he feels guilty for withdrawing. In his community, he is a man others expect to be strong, available, composed. He tries to perform that version of himself in public, but afterward he comes home shaking with tension, sometimes snapping at his wife over minor things and then sitting alone with regret.

Months pass, then longer, and he is surprised that the rawness does not fade the way people said it would. He still scans the road when loved ones are late returning home. He still checks his phone repeatedly, then feels a cold drop in his stomach when it rings unexpectedly. He keeps one of his brother's old voice notes and plays it at times when he is alone, needing to hear the ordinary sound of him. He says the worst part is not only that his brother is gone, but that the world afterward no longer feels safe or familiar. Even on calm days, he lives as if braced for another call that will change everything.
